source.title: What Makes Two Language Models Think Alike?
source.authors: Jeanne Salle; Louis Jalouzot; N. Lan; Emmanuel Chemla; Yair Lakretz

record.tranche_reason: The study directly compares language-model representations for convergence, but uses linguistic-feature signatures and Dynamic Time Warping rather than the original geometric similarity measures. It also compares its feature-based analysis with an RSA baseline.
record.gate_note: The study reports model-level and layer-level similarity results, plus selected cross-family layer comparisons. MLEM fit performance for individual layers is not recorded because it is not a cross-model similarity result. The closest and farthest layer-pair selection procedure is not itself a result.
record.test_reason: The study compares representations across language-model families and sizes using linguistic feature-importance signatures, rather than the original geometric alignment measures. Its results bear on scale-dependent convergence, partial convergence, and measurement dependence.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that different architecture classes can share linguistic signatures, while family and release date structure similarity more strongly than scale. They interpret convergence as partial rather than a single scale-driven endpoint; they do not establish causal explanations or directly test cross-modal convergence.
record.recipe_differences: Uses metric-learning encoding models to derive interpretable linguistic signatures, compares layer profiles with Dynamic Time Warping, and uses RSA only as a feature-agnostic baseline. The original claim is discussed through geometric alignment; this study's primary measure compares feature importance profiles.
record.method_sensitivity: The detected loop-like organization differs between linguistic-signature comparison and RSA. The study also restricts its analysis to a synthetic Relative Clause dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected Pythia–Mamba and Pythia–Mamba2 layers have highly similar linguistic signatures, with R² = 0.95 and 0.99.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different language-model architectures can organize sentence representations around similar explicit linguistic variables at selected layers.

record.problems: The analysis uses a synthetic dataset restricted to specific syntactic constructions; the authors say natural unconstrained text should be tested. Signatures cover only the specified linguistic features and whole layers, not units or circuits. The cross-family layer examples are selected illustrative comparisons. The study does not test cross-modal convergence.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported cross-model similarity results were left out. Individual-layer MLEM encoding performance in Figure S3 was omitted because it measures prediction of neural distances from features, not convergence between models.

untested.parts: Capability-dependent convergence, different training objectives, and a direct monotonic relationship between scale and raw geometric alignment are untested. All evaluated models use next-token prediction.
No paired image-caption representations or cross-modal improvement comparisons.
No controlled comparisons across random initializations.
No transfer maps, stitching, interchangeability, or performance-loss measurements.
No identification of recurring neurons, SAE features, or circuits; linguistic signatures summarize whole-layer organization.
No systematic metric-setting sweep or natural-text/out-of-distribution comparison. The metric comparison also changes visualization methods.
No scale-dependent plateau or causal demonstration that shared training data or objectives explain alignment. Signature differences do not quantify how far complete neural alignment remains.

missing.what: An exploratory input-representation comparison found that concatenating all token embeddings made pairwise distances depend on token identities rather than the intended linguistic features. This qualitative result bears on input-representation dependence; no numerical comparison is supplied.
missing.locator: Appendix B, Model Inventory and Experimental Setup, second paragraph

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for any version. Conclusions concern specified linguistic features on a synthetic dataset, rather than complete neural representations. Small Pythia models were excluded after near-floor exploratory encoding fits, which narrows the scale comparison; those fits themselves are not cross-model convergence results. Selected closest and farthest examples cannot establish typical cross-family similarity.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test independently trained models with different objectives or data modalities, and does not directly measure whether raw geometric alignment rises monotonically with size and capability.
Cross-modal image-caption alignment is explicitly outside the study; it analyzes language models on a syntactic sentence dataset.
No same-architecture comparisons across random seeds or initialization conditions.
Does not test representation mapping, stitching, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
Does not test recurrence of interpretable units, SAE features, neurons, or circuits.

Compares linguistic-signature similarity with RSA for a subset of models, but does not vary similarity settings or test out-of-distribution inputs. The authors identify the synthetic dataset's restricted constructions as a limitation but do not report a natural-text comparison.
Does not establish whether shared training data or objectives causally explain the observed similarities, or directly test whether alignment plateaus as scale increases.

rows.subject: 43 language models across 10 families
rows.operation_detail: Compared model-level layerwise linguistic-signature profiles using normalized multi-dimensional Dynamic Time Warping; used an MLEM to explain the resulting pairwise similarity structure.

conditions.value: 43 models across 10 families and 3 architecture classes

rows.measure: DTW distance between layerwise linguistic-signature profiles; feature importance of model properties for explaining the pairwise DTW matrix
rows.value: Release date was the strongest predictor of model-level linguistic-signature similarity, followed by family membership; parameter count, training-token count, and depth contributed less. Architecture class and depth-to-width ratio contributed little once the other properties were included.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation across the original 5-fold cross-validation is shown for feature-importance estimates; specific values not stated in the text.
rows.note: The authors interpret release date as a proxy for general LLM development. This is an aggregate analysis of the model set, not a reported single distance for each model pair.
rows.check: The result qualifies scale-driven convergence: release date and family explain more signature variation than parameter count. Predictor importance does not establish that alignment decreases with scale, remains far from complete, or has a particular causal explanation.

rows.subject: Language models grouped by family
rows.size_stated: 100M to 14B parameters across the evaluated set
rows.operation_detail: Compared layer-level linguistic-signature feature-importance vectors using Euclidean distance and visualized layer trajectories in a shared PCA space.

conditions.value: Layerwise linguistic signatures from last-token embeddings

rows.measure: Euclidean distance between layer-level feature-importance vectors; qualitative similarity of PCA trajectories
rows.value: Models from the same family trace similar layerwise trajectories, including models with substantially different parameter counts and numbers of layers. The authors state that these patterns suggest similarity is shaped by family rather than scale.
rows.note: This is evidence of family-structured similarity, not a reported monotonic increase in similarity with model size.
rows.check: Family-structured trajectories qualify uniform scale-driven convergence but do not measure a monotonic scale trend. Add V6 because these trajectories provide the feature-based comparator for r3.

source_check.locator_found: Sections 4.1–4.2; Figure 4 and caption; Figure S5 caption.

rows.subject: GPT-2, OPT, and Pythia models
rows.size_stated: 117M to 13B parameters across the included models
rows.operation_detail: Compared raw pairwise neural-distance matrices using RSA and projected the resulting similarities with MDS.
rows.measure: Spearman correlation between pairwise neural-distance matrices; qualitative MDS trajectories
rows.value: RSA also showed that models from the same family tend to follow similar trajectories, but the loop-like organization seen with linguistic signatures was weaker and was not clearly shown, even for GPT-2.
rows.note: The paper reports a difference in the structure made visible by the two similarity approaches; it does not report that RSA eliminates all family-level similarity.
rows.check: The measurement dependence appears: loops are weaker under RSA while family trajectories persist. This comparison also changes the projection from PCA to MDS, so it does not isolate the similarity metric alone.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, final paragraph; Figures S7–S8 and captions; Table S1.

rows.subject: Pythia-6.9B layer 14 and Mamba-790M layer 21
rows.operation_detail: Compared linguistic-signature feature-importance profiles for a selected cross-family layer pair.

conditions.value: Closest retained layer from another family to the reference layer
Relative Clause type was the leading shared feature

rows.value: R² = 0.95 ± 0.01; the authors describe the signatures as similar and report clear clustering by Relative Clause type in both neural spaces.
rows.note: The comparison is an illustrative selected pair, not a representative estimate across all cross-family layers.
rows.check: A selected highly similar layer pair establishes neither increasing alignment with scale nor incomplete convergence. The reported R² concerns linguistic signatures, not complete representational alignment.

rows.subject: Pythia-6.9B layer 14 and Qwen3-4B layer 16
rows.operation_detail: Compared linguistic-signature feature-importance profiles for a selected cross-family layer pair.

conditions.value: Farthest retained layer from another family to the reference layer
Relative Clause type was prominent in the reference but had low importance in the comparison layer

rows.value: R² = 0.58 ± 0.01; the authors describe the signatures as dissimilar and report little Relative Clause type organization in the Qwen3-4B layer.
rows.note: The paper notes this layer is much farther from the reference than the selected Mamba layer, despite Qwen3-4B being closer in architecture and parameter count.
rows.check: The selected dissimilar pair demonstrates incomplete agreement in linguistic organization. Remove V1: a single selected pair does not measure how alignment changes with size or capability. Selection was restricted to retained layers within the same relative-depth eighth.

rows.subject: Pythia-1.4B layer 8 and Mamba2-780M layer 14
rows.operation_detail: Compared linguistic-signature feature-importance profiles for a selected cross-family layer pair.

conditions.value: Closest retained layer from another family to the reference layer
Verb lemma contributed moderately in both layers

rows.value: R² = 0.99 ± 0.00; the authors describe the signatures as similar.
rows.note: The comparison is an illustrative selected pair, not a representative estimate across all cross-family layers.
rows.check: A selected highly similar layer pair establishes neither a scale trend nor incomplete convergence. Signature R² = 0.99 does not demonstrate complete alignment of neural representations.

rows.subject: Pythia-1.4B layer 8 and Qwen3-4B layer 11
rows.operation_detail: Compared linguistic-signature feature-importance profiles for a selected cross-family layer pair.

conditions.value: Farthest retained layer from another family to the reference layer
Verb lemma contributed much more strongly in the comparison layer

rows.value: R² = 0.46 ± 0.02; the authors describe the signatures as dissimilar and report sharper clustering by Verb lemma in the Qwen3-4B layer.
rows.note: The comparison is an illustrative selected pair, not a representative estimate across all cross-family layers.
rows.check: The selected dissimilar pair demonstrates incomplete agreement in linguistic organization. Remove V1 because no scale or capability trend is measured. Selection was restricted to retained layers within the same relative-depth eighth.

relationships.condition: Linguistic signatures of the 43 retained language models on synthetic relative-clause sentences
relationships.reason: Release date and family dominate the predictors, and within-family trajectories remain similar across sizes (r1, r2); this qualifies scale as the main explanation without establishing an absent or reversed scale trend.
relationships.display_finding: Family and release date dominated similarity predictors, while within-family linguistic trajectories remained similar across model sizes.

source_check.reason: r1 and r2 show family- and generation-structured similarity with smaller parameter-count contributions, qualifying a uniform scale-driven convergence account without establishing an absent or reversed scaling effect.

relationships.condition: Feature-based PCA versus RSA-based MDS for GPT-2, OPT, and Pythia layers
relationships.reason: Family trajectories persist, but loops visible in linguistic signatures are weaker under RSA (r2, r3), supporting dependence of the revealed structure on the analysis approach.
relationships.display_finding: Family trajectories persisted across analyses, while loops visible in linguistic signatures were weaker under RSA.

source_check.reason: r2 and r3 show similar family trajectories under both approaches but weaker loop structure under RSA-based MDS. This supports dependence on the analysis approach; changing both representation comparison and projection prevents isolating the similarity metric alone.

relationships.reason: Family and generation structure persist (r1, r2), and selected pairs differ in feature importance with R² = 0.58 and 0.46 (r5, r7), supporting partial convergence of linguistic organization.
relationships.display_finding: Family and generation structure persisted, and selected pairs differed in feature importance with R² values of 0.58 and 0.46.

relation.reason: Its own cross-model results address convergence, persistent family structure, and differences between feature-based and geometric comparisons.

tranche.reason: The study explicitly examines representational convergence using feature-based linguistic signatures and DTW, with RSA as a baseline, rather than the original geometric alignment approach.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v3 dated 4 June 2026, although the pack lists year 2024. Conclusions concern selected linguistic features on synthetic sentences; natural-text generalization, cross-modal convergence, and causal explanations remain untested.

statements.correction: V1: limits_scope. Release date is the strongest predictor of linguistic-signature similarity, followed by family; parameter count contributes less. Within-family signatures remain similar across sizes. No absent or reversed scale-alignment trend is established.
statements.problem: The factual description and explicit caveat about this study are accurate, but the statement's challenges label overstates its evidence against V1.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Model-level linguistic-signature similarities across the evaluated models
reader_labels.reason: The strongest predictors were release date and family rather than parameter count, and the authors state that the results do not support scale alone driving all models toward one endpoint (r1, r2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Some cross-family layer signatures were very similar while other selected pairs were substantially less similar, indicating structured and incomplete rather than uniform convergence (r4–r7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Feature-based linguistic signatures compared with RSA for GPT-2, OPT, and Pythia
reader_labels.reason: Both approaches show family-level trajectories, but the loop-like organization is weaker or not clearly visible with RSA, so the detected structure depends in part on the similarity measure (r2, r3).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Evaluated models and selected cross-family layer comparisons
reader_labels.reason: The results show partial, family- and generation-structured similarity rather than a single undifferentiated endpoint; selected cross-family layer signatures also vary substantially in similarity (r1, r2, r4–r7).
